1233.title: Faith has six parts
1233.hook: belief in Allah, His angels, books, messengers, the Last Day, and decree (Muslim)
1233.howItsDone: The six articles of faith are taught as a list, and the hadith of Jibril is taught as a summary of the religion in three layers: islam, iman and ihsan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fiqh close: the end of the long block on law. Your line: many roads, one direction.

The companions are sitting with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ when a man walks in. His clothes are brilliantly white, his hair very black, and there's no dust of travel on him. Nobody in the room knows who he is. He sits knee to knee with the Prophet, rests his hands on his own thighs, and starts asking questions. What is islam? The Prophet answers, and the stranger says, you have spoken truly. The companions, as Umar tells it, were amazed that he asked and then confirmed the answer himself. Then the second question: tell me about iman.
screen: `A STRANGER IN WHITE.` → `KNEE TO KNEE.` → `TELL ME ABOUT IMAN.`

segments.voice: Day five met the word itself, from a root of safety and trust. Today, what it holds. This scene is in Sahih Muslim, and the answer is a list. Iman, the Prophet says, is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and to believe in the decree, its good and its harm. Six, and this week takes them one at a time. First, the shape of the conversation. The stranger asks three things in order. Islam is answered with things you do: the testimony, prayer, charity, fasting, pilgrimage. Iman is answered with things you hold true. Ihsan is answered with how you worship: as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, knowing that He sees you. Body, belief and heart, in one sitting. Second, much of the list is already in the Qur'an. Pickthall's translation of one verse says of the believers: "Each one believeth in Allah and His angels and His scriptures and His messengers." The hadith gathers that together and adds the Last Day and the decree. Third, the stranger. After he leaves, the Prophet tells Umar it was Jibril, the angel Gabriel, come to teach the people their religion. An angel taught the list that includes the angels. Last, why a list. Six short items are easy to carry. A child can count them on one hand and one more finger; a scholar can spend a life on any one.
screen: `ISLAM, IMAN, IHSAN.` · `THE LIST IS IN THE QUR'AN TOO.` · `THE STRANGER WAS JIBRIL.` · then, large: `SIX TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: Hold up one hand and fold a finger down for each, slowly, aloud or in your head: Allah, the angels, the books, the messengers, the Last Day, and then the thumb of the other hand, the decree. Go through them once more, slower, and notice where your mind lingers; you don't have to say why.
Iman. Faith, belief: in the hadith of Jibril, belief in Allah, His angels, books, messengers, the Last Day, and the decree. Today's word.
Your line: six to believe. Tomorrow, the first of the six, and the shortest description of God. Peace until then.

1234.title: Allah, the One
1234.hook: one, eternal, merciful, like nothing else
1234.howItsDone: Muslims recite Surah al-Ikhlas often, in daily prayers and at other times, and the oneness of God, tawhid, stands at the center of Islamic belief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, iman, and your line: six to believe. Allah, angels, books, messengers, the Last Day, the decree.

How short can a description of God be? The Qur'an gives one in four short verses. The chapter is called al-Ikhlas, sincerity, and it sits near the very end of the book, small enough to learn in a sitting and said in prayer. Day one hundred sixty-two met the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says it equals a third of the Qur'an. Four verses, worth a third. Today they open the first article of faith.
screen: `HOW SHORT CAN IT BE?` → `FOUR VERSES.` → `EQUAL TO A THIRD.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in Pickthall's translation. "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him." A line at a time. First, one. Not one among several, and not the first of a series. Muslims call this tawhid, oneness, and it's the center of the whole list of six. Second, eternally besought. The Arabic word is as-Samad, and translators struggle with it. Pickthall's phrase points to the one everyone turns to, who needs nothing from anyone. Every other thing leans on something; this One doesn't lean. Third, nothing like Him. Another verse says it plainly: "Naught is as His likeness." Some readers see here one reason Islamic art leaves out pictures of God and turns to calligraphy and pattern instead. Fourth, merciful. The surah doesn't say it, but the line said before surah after surah does: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." Oneness in Islam isn't cold. And a word about the name. Allah is the Arabic word for God. Arabic-speaking Christians say Allah in their prayers and their Bibles, and Arabic-speaking Jews have used it as well. The name is shared; what Muslims say about Him is in those four verses.
screen: `ONE, NOT ONE OF MANY.` · `THE ONE ALL TURN TO.` · `NAUGHT IS AS HIS LIKENESS.` · then, large: `THE ONE IS MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: Notice how many things are in your mind right now, a message to answer, a sound outside, a worry, and let them be many. Then rest on one thing, your breath or the single word one, and come back to it each time the many pull you away. If you pray, you can recite al-Ikhlas slowly, or simply the word Allah; if not, the word one is enough.
Allah. The Arabic word for God; in the Qur'an, the One, the eternally besought, with none comparable unto Him. Today's word.
Your line: one. Tomorrow, the second article: the angels. That's today, done.

1235.title: The angels
1235.hook: created from light, obeying, never tiring
1235.howItsDone: Muslims end each prayer by turning the head right and left with the words peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah; belief in angels, including Jibril and the recording angels, is the second article of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Allah, the One, and your line: one. Four short verses, worth a third of the Qur'an.

Watch the end of any Muslim prayer. The person sitting on the floor turns the head to the right and says peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah. Then to the left, the same words. In a row, there's a person on each side, so the greeting lands somewhere. But some scholars say it's meant for more than the neighbors: it's also for the angels, the ones the Qur'an describes as noble recorders, keeping watch over every person. A small turn of the head, and a hello to the second article of faith.
screen: `RIGHT, THEN LEFT.` → `PEACE BE UPON YOU.` → `TO WHOM?`

segments.voice: Day six hundred sixty-five met the angels by name; today, why they're an article of faith. Start with what they're made of. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says the angels were created from light, the jinn from smokeless fire, and Adam from what you have been told: the earth. Three kinds of creature, three materials. Next, what they do. The Qur'an describes angels who carry out what they're commanded and do not disobey, and others who glorify Allah night and day without tiring. Some are known by name and task: Jibril, who brought the revelation, Mika'il, and the angel of death. Others record, others guard. Then a surprise. Obedient doesn't mean silent. In the second surah, Allah tells the angels, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." And the angels ask: will you put there someone who will do harm and shed blood, when we praise you? Allah answers that He knows what they don't. Adam is taught the names of things, and the angels admit they know only what they've been taught. The beings of light ask, and then they learn. Last, why believe in them at all. For Muslims, angels are part of how the unseen world works: revelation came through one, deeds are written by others, and no deed goes unwitnessed. That's held not as a mood but as the second of the six.
screen: `LIGHT, FIRE, EARTH.` · `THEY OBEY AND DON'T TIRE.` · `THE ANGELS ASKED A QUESTION.` · then, large: `NO DEED UNWITNESSED.`

segments.voice: Settle, then turn your head gently to the right and say, aloud or inside, peace be upon you; turn to the left and say it again. Then face forward and stay there. If you pray, this is the greeting you already know; if you don't, take it as a greeting to whatever company you keep, the people near you and whatever is unseen.
The angels. Mala'ikah in Arabic: created from light, obeying their Lord, glorifying Him without tiring. The second article of faith. Today's word.
Your line: made of light. Tomorrow, the third article of faith: the books. See you tomorrow, then.

1236.title: The books
1236.hook: the Torah of Musa, the Psalms of Dawud, the Gospel of Isa, the Scrolls of Ibrahim, and the Qur'an
1236.howItsDone: Muslims affirm belief in the revealed books, naming the Tawrat, Zabur, Injil, the scrolls of Ibrahim and the Qur'an, and a Qur'an at home may be kept on a high shelf, sometimes wrapped in cloth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the angels, and your line: made of light. A greeting to them at the end of every prayer.

Here's an unusual article of faith: it asks Muslims to believe in books that may never sit on their own shelves. The third of the six is the books, kutub in Arabic. Not only the Qur'an at home, perhaps wrapped in cloth on a high shelf. Also a scroll given to Ibrahim. A law given to Musa. Songs given to Dawud. A gospel given to Isa, the name the Qur'an uses for Jesus. Five books, five messengers, one belief that holds them together.
screen: `BOOKS NEVER ON THE SHELF.` → `FIVE BOOKS, FIVE MESSENGERS.`

segments.voice: First, the names. The Qur'an names the Tawrat, the Torah, given to Musa, Moses. The Zabur, the Psalms, given to Dawud, David; in Pickthall's words, "We imparted unto David the Psalms." The Injil, the Gospel, given to Isa. And at the end of a short surah, a fourth: "Lo! This is in the former scrolls, The Books of Abraham and Moses." With the Qur'an itself, that makes five. Second, how they connect. The Qur'an speaks of itself as confirming what was revealed before it, the Torah and the Gospel among them. In Muslim teaching the message across the books is the same at its heart: worship the One, do good, a day of reckoning is coming. Third, what the belief is and isn't. It's belief in those books as they were revealed to their messengers. The Qur'an is held to be the last book and the measure of the others, and Muslim scholars discuss how the earlier texts reached us. Jews and Christians read their own scriptures on their own terms; this path just says who holds what. Last, a phrase. In one verse the Arabic reads, word by word, for every term, a book. Pickthall renders it, "For everything there is a time prescribed." Some readers hear in it the same idea as this article of faith: no age was left without a word from its Lord.
screen: `TAWRAT, ZABUR, INJIL, SCROLLS.` · `CONFIRMING WHAT CAME BEFORE.` · `AS THEY WERE REVEALED.` · then, large: `FOR EVERY TERM, A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Picture a single shelf and set five books on it one by one, saying each name as you place it: the scrolls of Ibrahim, the Torah of Musa, the Psalms of Dawud, the Gospel of Isa, the Qur'an, brought to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Then look at the whole shelf for a while. If you pray, you can ask to understand what your own book asks of you; if not, just rest your eyes on the shelf.
Kutub. Books; the plural of kitab. The third article of faith: belief in the books Allah revealed to His messengers. Today's word.
Your line: every age had a book. Tomorrow, the people who carried them: the messengers. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1237.title: The messengers
1237.hook: a messenger was sent to every people (16:36)
1237.howItsDone: Muslims affirm belief in all of Allah's messengers, named and unnamed, and when a prophet's name is mentioned they commonly add a phrase asking peace upon him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kutub, the books, and your line: every age had a book. Today, the people who carried them.

"And verily We have raised in every nation a messenger." That's Pickthall's translation of a verse in the sixteenth surah, and it's a big sentence to sit inside. Every nation. Not just the ones whose stories reached a book you've read. The valley towns, the islands, the peoples on the far side of every map. Among each of them, the verse says, a messenger stood up and spoke. Today, the fourth article of faith, and the question it leaves open: who were they all?
screen: `IN EVERY NATION A MESSENGER.` → `NOT JUST THE FAMOUS ONES.` → `WHO WERE THEY ALL?`

segments.voice: First, the word. Rusul means messengers; one is a rasul, one who is sent. Scholars also use the word nabi, prophet. One common way they put it: every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger, since a messenger is sent with a message to deliver to a people. Second, the named. Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud, Isa, Yunus, Yusuf and more, ending with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, whom the Qur'an calls the seal of the prophets. The verse in the sixteenth surah also says what they came to say: worship Allah alone. Many voices, one core message. Third, the unnamed. Another verse tells the Prophet that some messengers' stories have been told to him, and some have not. So the Qur'an's list isn't the whole list. There are messengers whose names no Muslim knows, sent to peoples whose languages may be gone, and belief in them is still part of the fourth article. Last, how they're held. In the verse that lists the articles of faith, the believers say, in Pickthall's words, "We make no distinction between any of His messengers." The Qur'an also says some messengers were given gifts above others. But the belief takes in all of them, the ones with long stories and the ones with no story at all.
screen: `RUSUL: THOSE WHO ARE SENT.` · `MANY NAMED, ONE MESSAGE.` · `SOME NEVER NAMED.` · then, large: `NO DISTINCTION BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: Let your mind go somewhere far away and long ago, a mountain village, a fishing coast, a city whose name nobody remembers, and hold the thought that someone was sent there, speaking to their own people in a language you don't know. Then move to another place, and another. If you pray, you can send peace upon the messengers, as Muslims do when a prophet is named; if not, let each place go by in silence.
Rusul. Messengers; one is a rasul, one who is sent. The fourth article of faith: belief in all of Allah's messengers. Today's word.
Your line: every people had one. The named and the unnamed alike, every one of them sent. Rest well.

1238.title: The Last Day: raised and weighed
1238.hook: the resurrection, the reckoning, the garden and the fire
1238.carry: an atom's weight of good will be seen
1238.howItsDone: Belief in the Last Day is the fifth article of faith; Muslims recite al-Fatiha, which names Allah as master of the Day of Judgment, in prayer, and Surah Ya Sin may be read for the dying and the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rusul, the messengers, and your line: every people had one. Named or unnamed, every nation was sent someone.

Tradition says a man in Mecca picked up an old bone, crumbled it in his hand, and asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ a mocking question. Who's going to bring this back to life once it's rotted away? The Qur'an records the question, and the answer that comes back is very short: the one who made it the first time will make it again. That exchange sits near the end of Surah Ya Sin, and tradition links that surah with the dying and the dead.
screen: `A CRUMBLING BONE.` → `WHO BRINGS THIS BACK?` → `THE ONE WHO MADE IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: The word for it is akhirah, the hereafter, the life that comes last. The Qur'an keeps setting it beside dunya, this near world, the one we're in now. Belief in the Last Day has four movements. First, the resurrection. The bodies of the dead are raised, the bone in the man's hand included. The answer in Ya Sin argues from the first creation: making something again is no harder than making it at all. Second, the reckoning. Every life is laid open. Surah az-Zalzalah, a short surah about the earth shaking, ends with two lines: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." Nothing is too small to count, in either direction. Third, the two homes. The Qur'an describes a garden, with rivers, shade and peace, and a fire. It describes both vividly, and hides neither. Fourth, the One behind it. In the opening surah, al-Fatiha, Allah is called the Merciful and the master of the Day of Judgment in the same breath. Mercy and reckoning sit side by side. And this is why the Last Day sits among the six. For Muslims, it gives the ordinary day its weight: the kind word, the shortcut not taken, the atom of good nobody else saw.
screen: `THE BONES ARE RAISED.` · `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT.` · `A GARDEN AND A FIRE.` · then, large: `MERCIFUL, AND MASTER OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Think of meeting Him, or, if that isn't your language, of your life being seen whole. Bring up one small good thing from this week, a door held, a message answered kindly, and let it be seen; then one small harm, and let that be seen too, without arguing. If you pray, you can recite the opening surah slowly, with its two names, the Merciful and master of the Day; if not, just rest in being seen.
Akhirah. The hereafter, the life that comes last: the resurrection, the reckoning, the garden and the fire. The fifth article of faith. Today's word.
Your line: an atom's weight of good will be seen. Tomorrow, the sixth and final article of faith: the decree. Peace to you.

1239.title: The decree
1239.hook: all things happen by Allah's knowledge and will, the good and the hard
1239.howItsDone: Belief in qadar, the divine decree, is the sixth article of faith; when something hard happens, Muslims may say that Allah decreed it, and the advice to tie your camel and trust is quoted alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, akhirah, the Last Day, and your line: the last day. An atom's weight of good, and nothing too small to count.

A bus pulls away just as you reach the stop. A test result comes back. A call with good news, a call with bad. Moments like those come with a ready-made sentence, and it often starts with if only. A hadith in Sahih Muslim takes that phrase head on. When something befalls you, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says, don't say if only I had done this. Say: Allah decreed it, and He did what He willed. For if only, he says, opens the door to Satan's work.
screen: `A BUS PULLS AWAY.` → `IF ONLY…` → `ALLAH DECREED IT.`

segments.voice: The word is qadar, decree, measure. In the hadith of Jibril, the list of six ends with it: to believe in the decree, its good and its harm. First, the measure. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! We have created every thing by measure." Nothing is random to Allah's knowledge: what happens is known and willed, the easy days and the hard ones. Second, what the belief is for. Another passage says what is coming is already written, so that a person doesn't despair over what slipped away or get carried away by what was given. Qadar steadies both ends, the loss and the win. That's the work the if only hadith is doing. It doesn't say the bus didn't matter; it says the endless replay doesn't help. Third, what it doesn't mean. In a hadith in Tirmidhi's collection, a man asks whether to tie his camel or leave it loose and trust Allah. The answer: tie it, and trust. Decree isn't permission to stop trying. A person still plans, works, takes medicine, ties the camel. Fourth, the open question. How Allah's decree and human choice fit together is an old argument in Islamic theology, and Muslim schools answer it differently; this path meets those theologians soon. And that completes the six: Allah, the angels, the books, the messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
screen: `EVERY THING BY MEASURE.` · `NO DESPAIR, NO GLOATING.` · `TIE YOUR CAMEL, AND TRUST.` · then, large: `DECREE AND CHOICE: AN OPEN QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Find one if only that's been replaying lately, a medium one, not the biggest, and notice the sentence your mind keeps saying about it. Then gently say what happened, plainly, once: it happened, or, if you pray, Allah decreed it, and He did what He willed. Then notice what's still yours to do next. If a loss feels too heavy to carry, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Qadar. Decree, measure: belief that all things happen by Allah's knowledge and will, the good and the hard. The sixth article of faith. Today's word.
Your line: all by his decree. The camel still gets tied. See you tomorrow.
